screens.title: Kanban versus Scrum
screens.narratorSegment: Kanban and Scrum are both Agile-minded but they answer different organizational needs. Kanban is flow-based: it visualizes work, limits Work In Progress, and aims for a steady stream of value. Scrum is prescriptive: it defines roles, events, and timeboxed sprints to deliver increments. A concrete example: if bug reports arrive unpredictably, a Kanban team can pull high-priority bugs into the board as capacity becomes available; a Scrum team may triage and defer them into the next sprint planning. That difference matters because Kanban can be applied to existing roles and processes with minimal disruption, while Scrum asks teams to adopt specific ceremonies and role changes. A common misconception is that Kanban lacks discipline; in fact, Kanban replaces rigid ceremonies with explicit policies, WIP discipline, and metrics like lead time. Another contrast is how change is introduced: Scrum uses sprint retrospectives to inspect and adapt, while Kanban encourages continuous, evolutionary change and experiments driven by observed flow. Takeaway: choose Kanban when work is continuous and priorities shift often; choose Scrum when predictable iterations and defined roles give you cadence and predictability. How would your team handle an urgent production bug today?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Kanban versus Scrum
Comparison

Key differences

Structure
Scrum prescribes roles and events. Kanban starts with current roles and adds flow rules.
Cadence
Scrum uses fixed-length sprints; Kanban flows continuously and pulls work when capacity exists.

Practical example

Imagine urgent bug reports arriving at random. In Kanban, the bug waits in the backlog until a slot opens in development or testing. This prevents overload and keeps teams focused on finishing work. In Scrum, the team may need to interrupt a sprint, triage the bug, or defer it to the next sprint, adding context switches.
Misconception
Kanban is not unstructured. It relies on explicit policies, WIP discipline, and clear metrics.
Pro tip
If your team already has ceremonies and stable roles, start Kanban by visualizing current work and adding a WIP limit to one column.
Key Takeaway

Kanban complements existing roles and focuses on flow; Scrum creates a structured cadence with prescribed roles and events.

screens.title: Four core principles of Kanban — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Two of the four Kanban principles are especially important when you begin: 'Start with what you do now' and 'Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change.' The first principle means you do not throw away roles, titles, or tools to adopt Kanban. Instead, you map your existing workflow, then add visual signals and limits. For instance, if your team uses a shared spreadsheet or email triage, treat each open item as a candidate card and move it through stages you already use. The second principle — incremental change — says make small experiments, measure impact, and only then scale the change. A concrete example: try a one-week WIP limit in the 'In Progress' column and observe lead times; if it helps, keep the limit or adjust it slightly. A common misconception is that Kanban requires no management; instead, it shifts management toward improving system-level flow through measured experiments. The takeaway is that adopting Kanban is organizationally safe when you respect current practices and deliberately evolve them. What is one small experiment you could try this week to improve flow? Four core principles of Kanban — Part 1 means begin with your current workflow and adopt changes gradually through measured experiments.. In practical terms, start where you are; pursue evolutionary change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Four core principles
Definition

Start with what you do now

This principle keeps adoption low-friction. Map your current stages and work items, then introduce visual cards and policies without reassigning roles.
Concrete example
Convert your existing open tasks from email or spreadsheet into cards on a board, preserving who owns each task.
Misconception
Not changing roles does not mean no process change. Kanban asks you to add visibility and limits, not ignore improvement.

Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change

Small, measurable experiments reduce resistance and reveal real effects. Use metrics like lead time to judge success.
Experiment idea
Apply a temporary WIP limit for one week and compare lead time before and after.
Why it matters
Incremental change lets you keep what works and discard what doesn't based on data, not opinion.
Key Takeaway

Adopt Kanban without upheaval by mapping current work and running small, measurable experiments to improve flow.

screens.title: Four core principles of Kanban — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: The remaining two Kanban principles emphasize people and distributed ownership: 'Respect current roles, responsibilities, and titles' and 'Encourage acts of leadership at all levels.' Respecting roles means Kanban doesn't force a role change; designers, testers, and product owners keep their responsibilities while the team focuses on improving the flow of work. This reduces resistance because individuals are not being told to retrain into a new job overnight. Encouraging leadership at all levels means anyone can suggest flow improvements — not just managers. A practical example is a developer noticing repeated rework in testing and proposing a short experiment to expand the 'Definition of Ready' or add a checklist that reduces downstream defects. A common misconception is that leadership means formal authority; in Kanban leadership can be small acts like proposing a WIP adjustment, documenting a policy, or training a peer. The core insight is that Kanban combines respect for existing structure with empowerment to make incremental improvements, creating a culture where flow improvements can come from anywhere. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Respect roles & leadership

Respect current roles

Kanban does not create mandatory new roles. Retain responsibilities while changing system rules to improve flow.
Example
A tester keeps their testing responsibilities while the team adds a testing WIP limit to balance throughput.
Misconception
Respecting roles doesn't prevent process change; it simply avoids forced organizational restructuring.

Encourage leadership at all levels

Leadership in Kanban is about initiative: spotting bottlenecks, suggesting experiments, and documenting policies regardless of title.
Practical idea
Anyone can propose a one-week experiment such as changing the 'Definition of Ready' to reduce rework.
Why it matters
Distributed leadership creates faster experiments and continuous improvement because change does not wait for permission.
Key Takeaway

Preserve roles to reduce friction and empower everyone to propose small, measurable improvements that enhance flow.

screens.title: The six core practices of Kanban
screens.narratorSegment: Kanban uses six core practices to translate principles into day-to-day work. First, visualize the workflow by creating a board with columns representing stages and cards representing items. Second, limit Work In Progress so teams focus on finishing work before starting more. Third, manage flow actively by detecting slowdowns and smoothing movement through the system. Fourth, make process policies explicit so everyone knows the entry and exit criteria for each stage. Fifth, implement feedback loops—regular stand-ups focused on flow, service delivery reviews with stakeholders, and operations reviews to evaluate the system. Sixth, improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally: propose changes, run experiments, and use metrics to judge success. A concrete scenario: set up a five-column board, add a WIP limit to 'In Progress', run daily flow-focused standups for two weeks, and measure lead time for completed items. A common mistake is implementing visualization without WIP discipline: boards alone reveal problems but do not solve them. The core takeaway is that practices work together — visualization reveals queues, WIP limits impose discipline, and feedback plus experiments drive sustainable improvement. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Six core practices

Use this checklist to move from idea to action.
1. Visualize workflow
Create columns and cards to make work visible and measurable.
2. Limit WIP
Set maximums per column to reduce multitasking and finish work faster.
3. Manage flow
Watch movement, find slowdowns, and remove bottlenecks.
4. Make policies explicit

5. Implement feedback loops

6. Improve collaboratively

Concrete example

screens.title: Visualize the workflow: building a simple Kanban board
screens.narratorSegment: Visualization is the first practice because you cannot improve what you cannot see. A typical board uses columns such as Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review or Testing, and Done. Cards represent single work items: tasks, features, or bugs. When cards move across columns you see the system's state: clusters of cards reveal queues and potential bottlenecks. For example, a content team might use Ideas → Draft → Review → Edit → Publish. A useful exercise is to add five sample cards and watch which columns accumulate. Important visual cues include aging cards that stay too long in one column and columns that regularly exceed practical capacity. A common mistake is creating too many columns that split work too finely; keep stages meaningful. Make policies visible on the board: what does 'Ready for Review' mean? What must a card include before it can be pulled? These explicit rules reduce ambiguity and make it easier to run experiments. Takeaway: a clear board plus simple policies gives teams the data they need to manage flow. In practical terms, columns, cards, and the path to done. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Visualize the workflow

Kanban board example

Columns represent stages; cards represent work. Use meaningful, not excessive, columns.
Backlog
Ideas and requests
To Do
Ready to start
In Progress
Active work (apply WIP)
Review / Testing
Quality checks
Done
Shippable work
Concrete example
A content team: Ideas → Draft → Review → Edit → Publish. Watch where items pile up to find bottlenecks.
Common mistake
Too many columns fragment work and hide actual bottlenecks. Keep stages that reflect real handoffs or activities.
Make policies explicit
Document what 'Ready' and 'Done' mean for each column. For example, 'Ready for Review' may require a completed draft and unit tests passed.
Try this
Add five sample cards, then run a flow check after three days to note where cards age.

A clear board and explicit policies create the data you need to manage flow and run meaningful experiments.

screens.title: Limit Work In Progress (WIP)
screens.narratorSegment: Work In Progress limits are one of Kanban's most powerful levers. A WIP limit caps the number of items allowed in a column at once. The effect is simple but counterintuitive: by restricting how much you start, you force the system to focus on finishing existing items, which reduces context switching and often shortens lead time. For example, set the 'In Progress' limit to three. If three items are already active, the team cannot pull a fourth until one moves forward. Common mistakes include setting limits too high, which lets overload persist, or too low, which may starve downstream activities. Finding the right limit is empirical: start with a reasonable number, observe flow and lead time, then adjust. A concrete experiment is to track two-week lead time before and after applying a WIP limit. Also avoid overriding limits casually; honoring them is how you learn where systemic constraints exist. The takeaway: WIP limits create visible scarcity that focuses effort on finishing, not starting. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Limit Work In Progress

WIP limits explained

Limits set the maximum number of items allowed in a stage. Their purpose is to focus teams on completing work rather than starting too many items.
Example
If 'In Progress' has a WIP limit of 3 and three cards are active, the team must move one forward before pulling another.
Common mistakes
  • Setting limits too high, which fails to create focus.
  • Setting limits too low, starving downstream work.
  • Overriding limits habitually, which loses the learning opportunity.
How to choose a limit
Start small, measure lead time and throughput, then adjust. For individuals, a WIP of 1–2 is common; for teams, consider hands-on capacity by stage.
Try this experiment
Record lead time for two weeks, add a WIP limit, then compare lead time after two more weeks.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Managing flow and identifying bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: Managing flow means actively watching how cards move and intervening when items stall. Bottlenecks show as columns with persistent queues or long-lived cards. The goal is to reduce the time it takes for an item to travel from request to delivery. Useful metrics are lead time, which measures that end-to-end duration, and throughput, the count of items completed in a period. A concrete example: if 'Testing' consistently has twice as many cards as other stages, testing is the bottleneck. Actions include investigating root causes — insufficient testers, slow test processes, or quality issues upstream — and then running experiments such as cross-training developers to assist testing, adding test automation, or temporarily adjusting WIP limits to rebalance flow. A common misconception is to blame individuals; Kanban directs attention to systemic causes so you can improve the process rather than punishing people. The takeaway is to diagnose with observable data, design a small experiment, and measure the effect on lead time and throughput. Identify bottlenecks

Look for columns with persistent queues and cards that age. These are signals a stage lacks capacity or has inefficient work.
Metrics
Lead time: total time from request to delivery. Throughput: items completed per period. Use these to measure the effect of experiments.
Example
If Testing has many queued cards, consider cross-training or automation, or lower upstream WIP to balance flow.

screens.title: Make process policies explicit

The practical takeaway is to start with a few essential policies that address frequent causes of rework and to update them as experiments reveal better approaches. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Explicit Policies

Why policies matter

Policies set the conditions that must be true before work moves. They reduce ambiguity and rework.
Example policy
'Ready for Test' requires a passing unit test, required documentation, and an assigned reviewer.
Misconception
Policies are not bureaucracy if they prevent rework and speed delivery; keep them concise and practical.

How to use policies

Write policies visibly on the board, apply them consistently, and treat them as experiment parameters you can adjust.
Try this
Make one policy for 'Definition of Ready' and run it for two sprints or two weeks, then measure changes in rework and lead time.

Explicit, minimal policies increase predictability and make experiments measurable.

screens.title: Feedback loops and continuous improvement
screens.narratorSegment: Kanban uses feedback loops to keep improvements grounded in actual performance. Flow-focused standups look at blockages and commitments, service delivery reviews involve stakeholders to align expectations, and operations reviews assess system-level performance. Continuous improvement is experimental: propose a change, run it, measure the impact on lead time or throughput, and then decide whether to keep, adjust, or discard it. For example, if you suspect testing is slow, you might run a two-week experiment to cross-train developers to help testing and measure throughput changes. A common misconception is that feedback loops equal long meetings. Kanban encourages short, focused interactions targeted at flow problems. The practical takeaway is to pick one feedback loop to run consistently, use simple metrics to judge experiments, and treat every change as reversible. This scientific approach turns observations into reliable process improvements over time. screens.title: Setting up a personal Kanban board
screens.narratorSegment: Let's put Kanban into practice with a personal board. First, define simple workflow stages such as Backlog (Ideas), To Do, In Progress, Review/Practice, and Done. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Personal Kanban

Activity: set up your personal Kanban

Follow these practical steps to manage your study tasks and measure improvement.
1. Define stages
Backlog → To Do → In Progress → Review/Practice → Done. Keep it simple.
2. List tasks
Add 5–7 concrete learning tasks like reading chapters, watching videos, or practicing commands.
3. Set WIP limits
For solo study, use WIP 1–2. Only pull more when slots open.

Measure lead time for two completed tasks over two weeks and note changes after adjusting WIP.

Backlog: Read Module 1. To Do: Watch Module 3 on Scrum. In Progress (WIP:2): Practice Git, Complete Module 2 quiz.

A small personal Kanban with a conservative WIP limit will increase focus and give measurable improvements in completion time.

Lead time measures how long a single item takes from request to delivery, which tells you customer-facing speed. Also remember the pull system: items are pulled into the next stage only when there's capacity, not pushed regardless of it. Finally, explicit policies are the rules that make transitions repeatable. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll unpack Kanban as a lightweight, practical approach to managing work. Kanban focuses on visual signals, limiting Work In Progress, and improving the flow of value from request to delivery. You will learn what makes Kanban different from time-boxed frameworks, how to apply its four guiding principles, and the six practices teams use to find and fix bottlenecks. Kanban is deliberately incremental: you start with what you already do and evolve the process experimentally. That makes it especially useful for teams with continuous incoming work or shifting priorities. As we proceed you'll see a simple Kanban board example, a clear explanation of WIP limits, and a hands-on activity to set up a personal board. By the end you will be able to describe why limiting WIP helps reduce multitasking, how visualization reveals hidden queues, and how small process experiments drive lasting improvements. Think about a task you are currently juggling: imagine it as a card moving toward done. Where might it get stuck, and what small change could nudge it forward?

Across these objectives you will learn both what Kanban asks you to do and why it changes outcomes. First, we'll explain Kanban's core principles so you can adopt the method without unnecessary disruption. You'll learn how starting with your current process and pursuing small, evolutionary changes reduces resistance and supports continuous improvement. Second, you'll study the six core practices, such as visualizing workflow and limiting work in progress, and learn why each practice is essential for steady delivery. Third, you'll practice reading and using a Kanban board so you can spot queues and bottlenecks quickly. Visualizing work changes how teams coordinate day to day. Finally, you'll master WIP limits: how to choose sensible limits, the common mistakes teams make, and how limits improve focus and shorten lead time. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify you've internalized the skill. By the end you'll be able to set up a basic personal Kanban board, apply WIP limits, and run small experiments that improve flow.

Now we'll clarify how to show you've achieved each objective. For explaining core principles, you will be able to list each principle and argue why 'start with what you do now' reduces organizational disruption, using a real example from your team or workflow. For the six practices, you will map each practice to a real activity on a board, for instance assigning a WIP limit and describing how that limit changes day-to-day behavior. For using a Kanban board, you will create a simple board with stages and five items, then identify at least one visible bottleneck and suggest a corrective experiment. Finally, for WIP limits you will set a limit, measure lead time for two items, and reflect on how the limit changed completion speed. Each milestone is practical: they ask you to act, observe, measure, and iterate. This procedural verification reinforces that Kanban is an empirical method — you change things, measure impact, and adjust. When you complete these milestones you'll have both conceptual understanding and applied experience.

Kanban and Scrum are both Agile-minded but they answer different organizational needs. Kanban is flow-based: it visualizes work, limits Work In Progress, and aims for a steady stream of value. Scrum is prescriptive: it defines roles, events, and timeboxed sprints to deliver increments. A concrete example: if bug reports arrive unpredictably, a Kanban team can pull high-priority bugs into the board as capacity becomes available; a Scrum team may triage and defer them into the next sprint planning. That difference matters because Kanban can be applied to existing roles and processes with minimal disruption, while Scrum asks teams to adopt specific ceremonies and role changes. A common misconception is that Kanban lacks discipline; in fact, Kanban replaces rigid ceremonies with explicit policies, WIP discipline, and metrics like lead time. Another contrast is how change is introduced: Scrum uses sprint retrospectives to inspect and adapt, while Kanban encourages continuous, evolutionary change and experiments driven by observed flow. Takeaway: choose Kanban when work is continuous and priorities shift often; choose Scrum when predictable iterations and defined roles give you cadence and predictability. How would your team handle an urgent production bug today?

Two of the four Kanban principles are especially important when you begin: 'Start with what you do now' and 'Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change.' The first principle means you do not throw away roles, titles, or tools to adopt Kanban. Instead, you map your existing workflow, then add visual signals and limits. For instance, if your team uses a shared spreadsheet or email triage, treat each open item as a candidate card and move it through stages you already use. The second principle — incremental change — says make small experiments, measure impact, and only then scale the change. A concrete example: try a one-week WIP limit in the 'In Progress' column and observe lead times; if it helps, keep the limit or adjust it slightly. A common misconception is that Kanban requires no management; instead, it shifts management toward improving system-level flow through measured experiments. The takeaway is that adopting Kanban is organizationally safe when you respect current practices and deliberately evolve them. What is one small experiment you could try this week to improve flow? In practical terms, start where you are; pursue evolutionary change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The remaining two Kanban principles emphasize people and distributed ownership: 'Respect current roles, responsibilities, and titles' and 'Encourage acts of leadership at all levels.' Respecting roles means Kanban doesn't force a role change; designers, testers, and product owners keep their responsibilities while the team focuses on improving the flow of work. This reduces resistance because individuals are not being told to retrain into a new job overnight. Encouraging leadership at all levels means anyone can suggest flow improvements — not just managers. A practical example is a developer noticing repeated rework in testing and proposing a short experiment to expand the 'Definition of Ready' or add a checklist that reduces downstream defects. A common misconception is that leadership means formal authority; in Kanban leadership can be small acts like proposing a WIP adjustment, documenting a policy, or training a peer. The core insight is that Kanban combines respect for existing structure with empowerment to make incremental improvements, creating a culture where flow improvements can come from anywhere. A few more terms help you measure and communicate improvements. Flow refers to the smooth movement of work items through the system. Lead time measures how long a single item takes from request to delivery, which tells you customer-facing speed. Throughput counts how many items you complete in a given period and helps detect capacity changes. Use these metrics to evaluate experiments: decreasing lead time or increasing throughput without harming quality means a positive change. Also remember the pull system: items are pulled into the next stage only when there's capacity, not pushed regardless of it. Finally, explicit policies are the rules that make transitions repeatable.
